subject: Agriculture
title: Crop Rotation Basics
description: A short lesson to help you apply Crop Rotation Basics.

hook.text: Planting the same crop on the same field every year exhausts the soil. Medieval farmers had a fix.

buildup.text: The two-field system alternated: grow wheat one year, leave the field fallow the next to recover.

discovery.text: The three-field system was better—wheat, then oats or barley, then fallow. One-third rested instead of half.

twist.text: This seemingly small change boosted output by 50%. More food meant more people, more villages, more trade.

climax.text: Three-field rotation spread across Europe by 1000 CE and powered the population boom of the High Middle Ages.

punchline.text: A third field changed the math—and fed a continent.

quiz.question: How did the three-field system improve on the two-field system?
options: Only one-third of land rested instead of half, boosting yields by 50%

details.summary: Crop rotation alternates different crops on the same land across seasons to maintain soil fertility and reduce pest buildup. This topic covers the evolution of rotation systems from medieval Europe to modern four-course rotations that eliminated the need for fallow.
details.whyItMatters: Before crop rotation, farmers had to leave fields fallow every other year, wasting half their land. Rotation doubled productive acreage and was one of the most important agricultural innovations in history.
takeaways: Medieval two-field systems left half the land fallow each year
Three-field rotation increased productive land from 50% to 67%
Adding turnips and clover as rotation crops eliminated fallow entirely

faq.question: How did crop rotation develop historically?
faq.answer: Ancient farmers noticed yields declined under continuous cropping and began alternating crops or leaving fields fallow. Medieval Europeans developed three-field rotation, and 18th-century innovators like Townshend created four-course systems eliminating fallow.

faq.question: Why is crop rotation better than growing the same crop continuously?
faq.answer: Different crops use different nutrients and host different pests. Rotation prevents nutrient depletion, breaks pest and disease cycles, adds diversity to root structures improving soil, and when legumes are included, adds free nitrogen.
